title: Projectivity and pure curve fibres for a finite relative factor
statement:
Let $k$ be a field and let $S,X,T,Y$ be integral finite-type $k$-schemes. Let $f:X	o S$ be H-projective, with $S/k$ H-projective and every geometric fibre of $f$ pure of dimension one. Let $q:T	o S$ and $
u:Y	o X$ be finite surjective $k$-morphisms. Suppose $g:Y	o T$ is a dominant $k$-morphism with $q\circ g=f\circ
u$ and that the induced morphism $h=(
u,g):Y	o X	imes_ST$ is finite. Suppose the generic fibre of $g$ over $k(T)$ is nonempty and pure of dimension one. Then $X,Y,T$ are H-projective over $k$, and $g$ is H-projective. At every $y\in Y$ the local topological dimension of its fibre for $g$ is at least one. Every geometric fibre of $g$ is pure of dimension one. No flatness of $f$ or $g$, and no normality of these schemes, is assumed.

H-projective means factoring as a closed immersion into a finite-dimensional projective space over the target followed by its projection [def-kun-projective]. Pure dimension one means that every irreducible component has topological Krull dimension one [def-weil-pure-dimension]. The local topological dimension at a point is the infimum of dimensions of its open neighbourhoods; this is not the dimension of its local ring. Dominant means having dense image. The remaining notions used are [def-weil-field], [def-pc-integral-scheme], [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], [def-sc-function-field], [def-pc-fibre-product].

proof.text: Compose the H-projective maps $X\to S\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ to obtain H-projectivity of $X/k$. Apply the affine-base clause of finite-over-projective to $Y\to X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ and to $T\to S\to\operatorname{Spec}k$: the base is affine Noetherian and the finite-type $k$-schemes $X,S$ are quasi-compact, so the required global projective embeddings are available. This proves H-projectivity of $Y/k,T/k$. Projectivity makes $S/k$ and $T/k$ proper, hence separated. Apply the finite-constant projective graph theorem with $F=k$, $R=Y$ (closed in some $\mathbf P^N_k$), the separated $k$-scheme $T$ and $c=g$: the graph $(i,g):Y\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^N_T$ is a closed immersion over $T$, so $g$ is H-projective, and (taking $S'=T$) $g$ is proper. The same theorem with $R=X$, the separated $k$-scheme $S$ and $c=f$ shows that $f$ is proper.

proof.text: The composite of $g$ with $T\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is locally of finite type by hypothesis; finite-type cancellation makes $g$ locally of finite type. Step 1 makes $g$ and $f$ proper, hence of finite type. Base change therefore makes each ordinary or geometric fibre of $g$ and of $f$ of finite type over its field. All these fibres are Noetherian, since a field is Noetherian. These observations supply the finite-type and Noetherian hypotheses in the following steps.

Let $\xi$ be the generic point of the integral scheme $Y$ and $\eta$ that of $T$, supplied by sobriety. Every nonempty open of $Y$ contains $\xi$. Continuity gives $g(Y)\subseteq\overline{\{g(\xi)\}}$; dominance and uniqueness of generic points imply $g(\xi)=\eta$. Thus $\xi$ corresponds to a point $\widetilde\xi$ of $Y_\eta$, using the fibre projection homeomorphism onto $g^{-1}(\eta)$. The given pure dimension one of $Y_\eta$ and the equidimensional-open local-dimension theorem, applied with the whole fibre as its open subset, give $\dim_{\widetilde\xi}Y_\eta=1$.

For $y\in Y$ write $d(y)=\dim_{\widetilde y}Y_{g(y)}$. The locus $U_0=\{y:d(y)\leq0\}$ is open by the local-fibre-dimension openness theorem, applicable by step 2. Step 3 shows $\xi\notin U_0$. Since any nonempty open of $Y$ contains $\xi$, $U_0$ is empty. Local dimension at an actual point is nonnegative, so $d(y)\geq1$ for every $y\in Y$. This is the asserted ordinary-fibre local lower bound; it uses neither flatness nor normality.

Fix a geometric point $\bar t:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to T$ and put $B=Y\times_T\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$, $C=X\times_S\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$, using $q\bar t$ for the second map. Associativity of fibre products identifies $B\to C$ with the base change of $h:Y\to X\times_ST$, so it is finite. For each $b\in B$ with image $y\in Y$, fibre-dimension invariance under base change identifies $\dim_b B$ with $d(y)$, hence gives $\dim_b B\geq1$. The given geometric-fibre hypothesis makes $C$ pure of dimension one. If $B$ is empty the purity conclusion is vacuous; otherwise $C$ is nonempty. Applying the equidimensional-open theorem to $C$, followed by the supremum-of-local-dimensions formula, gives $\dim C=1$.

For every $c\in C$, the scheme-theoretic fibre $B_c$ of $B\to C$ is finite over $\kappa(c)$ by finite base change. The finite-over-field theorem writes it as $\operatorname{Spec}D$ with $D$ finite-dimensional over $\kappa(c)$. Apply the finite-algebra discrete-spectrum theorem to the local ring $R=\kappa(c)$, whose only prime is zero: $\operatorname{Spec}D$ is finite discrete. An irreducible nonempty closed subset of a discrete space is a singleton, so its dimension is zero when nonempty; when empty its dimension is $-\infty$. Thus every $B_c$ has dimension at most zero.

source.place: 06RS (lemma-local-dimension-zero-henselian), proof, finite algebra over a dimension-zero local ring; morphisms.tex 01WH (definition-integral), 01WL (lemma-base-change-finite)

proof.text: Apply the fibre-and-image dimension bound to the $\Omega$-morphism $B\to C$: both schemes are finite type over $\Omega$ by step 2, $\dim C\leq1$ by step 5, and all its fibres have dimension at most zero by step 6. With $d=1,n=0$ it gives $\dim B\leq1$. The whole $B$ is an open neighbourhood of any $b\in B$, so $\dim_bB\leq\dim B\leq1$. Together with step 5 this gives $\dim_bB=1$ everywhere. The constant-local-dimension component theorem applies because $B$ is Noetherian by step 2. Every irreducible component of $B$ therefore has dimension one, as required. The empty case was already handled in step 5.

tool_uses.why: Step 1 composes the two global projective-space embeddings for X/S/k. This is a general projectivity tool, not an alternative to the alteration construction of this unit.
Step 1 uses only the affine-base conclusion over Spec k, first for Y over X and then for T over S. The unit has no finite-cover projectivity theorem of its own.

Step 1 uses projective implies proper to obtain separatedness of S/k and T/k for the graph theorem; step 2 then uses properness of f and g to get finite type. This general implication does not replace an alteration step.
Step 2 uses precisely clause (f), cancellation of local finite type from Y/k through T/k. It is a general scheme-morphism tool absent from the unit.
Step 2 uses finite-type base change to ordinary and geometric fibres. This is a general property of finite-type morphisms, not a replacement of the alteration route.
Step 2 applies finite type over a Noetherian base to the field-valued fibres. The unit has no separate Noetherianity theorem.
Step 3 obtains the unique generic points of the integral schemes Y and T. Scheme sobriety is a general topological tool, not a curve-alteration assertion.
Steps 3 and 5 convert componentwise purity of the generic fibre and C into pointwise local topological dimension. This generic dimension comparison is not supplied by the unit.
Step 4 uses the upstairs open locus of fibre dimension at most zero to propagate the generic lower bound. This general local-finite-type theorem is not a curve-factor purity assertion.
Steps 5 and 6 base change the assumed finite h, and then its geometric-base-change map to each residual fibre. The unit has no finite-base-change theorem of its own.
Step 5 uses equality of local topological fibre dimensions after geometric base change. This general dimension invariance is not supplied by the alteration construction.
Step 5 deduces dim C = 1 from constant local dimension and nonemptiness. This general topological identity is absent from the unit.
Step 6 writes a finite fibre over kappa(c) as the spectrum of a finite-dimensional algebra. This general affine algebra description does not assert the item or any purity clause.
Step 6 applies this finite-algebra theorem with R = kappa(c) to prove discrete zero-dimensional fibres. This is a general algebraic input, not a curve-factor purity theorem.
Step 7 uses only the second inequality, with d = 1 and n = 0, for B to C. The unit gives no general finite-type fibre/image dimension estimate.
Step 7 converts constant local dimension on the Noetherian geometric fibre B into componentwise purity. It is a general topological conversion and does not establish the preceding dimension bounds.
